common_name: Giant Pelican Flower (Brazilian Dutchman's Pipe, Calico Flower)

planting.note: Set out potted plants in spring once nights stay warm, giving the twining vine a sturdy arbor or wire support to climb; it needs consistent moisture and rich, well-drained soil to fuel its rapid growth.

directions: Plant in rich, well-drained soil next to a strong trellis or arbor, watering deeply and regularly through the growing season since this vine is a heavy feeder that grows fast in warmth and humidity. It produces enormous, mottled maroon-and-cream pouch-shaped flowers with a long tail-like tip that give off a faint carrion scent to lure pollinating flies, blooming heavily from summer into fall. Where winters are too cold to leave it outdoors it can be grown in a large container and overwintered in a bright, frost-free space, and it also serves as a larval host plant for pipevine swallowtail butterflies. Prune in late winter to control size and encourage fresh flowering growth.

common_name: Bill MacKenzie Clematis (Golden Bell Tangutica Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below soil level and roots shaded, then let the twining vine climb a fence, arbor, or large shrub in full sun.

directions: Give this vigorous clematis a large support to scramble over and keep its roots cool with mulch or low companion plants while the top growth reaches into full sun. Nodding, bell-shaped, bright yellow flowers with thick waxy petals appear from midsummer well into fall, followed by fluffy silvery seed heads that extend garden interest into winter. Because it flowers on new wood, cut the whole vine back hard to about a foot from the ground in late winter to keep it dense and floriferous rather than bare-legged. It is one of the toughest and most vigorous of the small-flowered clematis, tolerant of poor soil once established.

common_name: Duchess of Albany Clematis (Pink Tulip Texas Clematis)

planting.note: Set out in spring with the crown planted a couple of inches deep and the roots shaded, allowing the slender stems to twine up a trellis, obelisk, or fence in full sun.

directions: Grow this heritage cultivar of the Texas native clematis on a narrow support such as an obelisk or wire trellis, keeping its roots cool and shaded beneath low plantings. From midsummer into fall it produces slender, tulip-shaped, deep pink flowers with a candy-striped reverse that nod outward from the wiry stems rather than facing up, a distinctive habit inherited from its Texas parent species. Because it blooms on new growth, cut the vine back hard to a foot or so above the ground each late winter to renew vigor. It is more heat- and drought-tolerant than many large-flowered clematis, making it a good choice for warmer gardens.

planting.note: Plant in spring with the crown set a couple of inches below the soil surface and the base shaded, giving the vine a sturdy fence, pergola, or large shrub to climb into full sun.

directions: Plant with the roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs a trellis, arbor, or fence in full sun, watering regularly during dry spells to keep flowering strong. This long-blooming, vigorous cultivar produces large, glowing magenta-red flowers with contrasting golden anthers from midsummer through early fall, one of the most reliable and free-flowering of the older large-flowered hybrids. Because it blooms on both old and new wood, it only needs light shaping in late winter rather than a hard cutback, so leave the framework mostly intact when pruning. Its strong constitution and heat tolerance make it a dependable choice for covering fences and arbors quickly.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring with the crown a couple of inches deep and roots shaded, then train the twining stems onto a trellis or obelisk positioned so the top of the vine reaches full sun.

directions: Give this compact clematis a modest trellis or obelisk to climb, keeping the root zone shaded and moist while the top growth flowers in full sun to light shade. Its claim to fame is an unusually long-lasting, fully double flower packed with narrow rose-pink petals layered into a tight rosette, blooming from early summer and often repeating into fall as temperatures cool. Because it flowers on both old and new stems, it needs only a light tidy-up in late winter rather than hard pruning, so remove dead or weak growth and leave the rest. The dense, ruffled blooms make it a standout specimen for a container trellis or small garden support.

planting.note: Plant in spring or early fall with the crown a couple of inches below soil level and the roots shaded, letting the fine stems twine over a low fence, shrub, or wire support.

directions: Plant this cold-hardy species with its roots cool and shaded, ideally at the base of a low fence, wall, or open shrub for the wiry stems to scramble through. It is among the earliest clematis to bloom, opening nodding, lantern-shaped blue-purple to pink flowers on bare stems before most other vines have leafed out, followed by fluffy seed heads. Since it flowers on the previous year's growth, prune only lightly right after flowering to remove dead wood, never cutting it back hard. Its small scale and dainty flowers suit rock gardens, low trellises, or mixed borders where a larger clematis would be too much.

planting.note: Set out container plants in spring against a fence, arbor, or trellis in full sun to light shade, watering well until established in well-drained soil.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil next to a fence, arbor, or pergola so the twining stems have something sturdy to climb, and water regularly the first season while roots establish. Clusters of tubular, richly fragrant cream to pale yellow flowers open in late spring and early summer, gradually deepening to orange as they age, and are followed by small red berries that draw songbirds. It is a vigorous, semi-evergreen to deciduous climber that tolerates heat, dry spells, and poor soil once established, making it useful for covering a large structure quickly. Prune after flowering to keep it in bounds, since it can grow rampantly in favorable conditions.

common_name: Lady Margaret Passionflower (Red Hybrid Passion Vine)

planting.note: Plant out after the last frost in a warm, sheltered spot with a trellis or wire support, in rich, well-drained soil that stays evenly moist.

directions: Give this fast-growing hybrid a wire trellis, obelisk, or fence in a warm, sheltered spot, and keep the soil evenly moist but well drained. It bears an abundance of small, richly colored deep red-and-pink flowers with a dark maroon-purple center almost continuously from late spring until frost, drawing butterflies and hummingbirds to the garden. In frost-free climates it stays semi-evergreen and can be left to cover a large structure, while in cooler areas it is best grown in a container and brought indoors or treated as a fast annual climber. Cut back hard in late winter where it is hardy to keep new growth vigorous and floriferous.

common_name: Eden Climbing Rose (Pierre de Ronsard Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in spring in a sunny spot with rich, well-drained soil, spacing them well from walls or fences to allow air movement, and tie the canes to a support as they grow.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, tying the long canes to a fence, pillar, or arbor as they extend since this rose does not climb on its own. Large, cupped, old-fashioned-style blooms open cream at the center and blush to soft pink toward the outer petals, opening in flushes from late spring through fall with a light fragrance. It is noted for glossy, disease-resistant foliage that holds up well through summer heat and humidity compared to many older climbers. Prune lightly after the first flush to shape the plant and remove spent blooms, saving harder structural pruning for late winter dormancy.

planting.note: Set out container plants in spring against a trellis, fence, or arbor in full sun to part shade, in well-drained soil, and water regularly until roots establish.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil beside a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence, since this fast-scrambling vine needs support to weave through and will sprawl if left unstaked. Loose clusters of star-shaped white flowers with bright yellow centers open almost continuously from spring through fall in mild climates, giving off a light sweet fragrance especially in the evening. It is a vigorous, semi-evergreen climber that can be cut back hard in late winter to control its size and encourage fresh flowering shoots. Where winters bring hard freezes it dies back to the roots but often resprouts in spring, or it can be grown in a large container and moved to shelter.
sources: University of California Master Gardener Program
